newsitem.title: TURKEY: Velayati visit is headache for Turkey's Erbakan.
newsitem.headline: Velayati visit is headache for Turkey's Erbakan.

text.p: Some of Turkey's secularist newspapers, waiting to pounce on any hint of Islamist militancy in the government, accused Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan of going soft on Iran during a visit by Tehran's top diplomat.

Diplomats said Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati's two-day visit helped towards ending a diplomatic crisis that led to tit-for-tat expulsions, one of several potentially serious rows in recent years that has been contained.
But Erbakan was lambasted in the mainstream press on Tuesday for not taking a hard line against Velayati in a spat over the Islamic republic's alleged support for Islamist militancy in Turkey.
"Hoca apologises to Iran," the Radikal daily said in a banner headline.

Erbakan, known as Hoca (Teacher), is already under pressure to crack down on Moslem religious activism in a wave of official anti-Islamist feeling encouraged by Iran's insensitivity to Turkey's officially secular state.

The secularists who dominate Turkey's military, media and opposition have raged against Erbakan's Welfare Party since the Iranian ambassador made an Islamist speech at an event organised by the party in the Ankara district of Sincan in January.

Ambassador Mohammad Reza Bagheri allegedly urged the establishment of Islamic rule in Turkey. He and two other Iranian representatives who were accused of criticising Turkey's rigid secularist system later quit Turkey in a round of tit-for-tat expulsions.

Diplomats said the two sides arrived at some common ground during Velayati's visit that ended on Tuesday and the situation was resolved by agreement that empty ambassador seats in both capitals should be filled.

"The two countries have joint interests," Milliyet newspaper columnist Sami Kohen told Reuters. "There are, of course, economic interests. Turkey wants Iranian gas and Iran sees Turkey as its gateway to Europe."

Although Velayati seems to have succeeded in papering over the row with the Turkish Foreign Ministry, a bastion of pro-Western secularists, academic Dogu Ergil said Erbakan would lose points for not being seen to be tougher on Velayati.
"We have a dispute with Iran about the regime, about democracy and about power in the region," Ergil said.
"If our government tries to make it look as if there is no problem with Iran they will not be looked upon kindly by the people or the army."
The Iranian diplomats' comments that sparked the row were one link of a chain of events that led the secularist army to order the government 10 days ago to clamp down on Islamist activity.
"The Iranians haven't done (Erbakan) any favours," a foreign diplomat said. "They just made a mess of it."

The diplomat said Tehran had underestimated army fears that Iran was attempting to provoke Islamist unrest in Turkey. "They don't have good contacts here in the military...they just misjudged the feeling here."
The Turkish army is also uneasy about what it says is Iran's efforts to stockpile weapons of mass destruction and its support for Kurdish rebels in southeast Turkey.
Turkish armed forces' second highest commander General Cevik Bir criticised Iran's military build up at a speech in Washington two weeks ago.

Sunni Moslem Turkey and Shi'ite Iran have vied for regional influence for centuries. Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution gave the rivalry an added edge as a competition between a pro-Western democracy and militant Islamists.
In contrast to Erbakan, Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller were reported to have lectured Velayati on interfering in Ankara's domestic affairs.
"It's as if there are two governments," the Hurriyet daily wrote. "Erbakan was apologetic," it said. The prime minister thanked Velayati for his "understanding" during the dispute.
